sentences.text: All species of this extinct genus measured between 3 and 5 meters in length.
One specific specimen, cataloged as PMO 222.655, was estimated to be between 3.8 and 4.3 meters long.
The animal possessed a very short but robust snout relative to the total length of its skull.
Its eye socket was approximately 0.34 times the length of the skull.
The shaft of the upper arm bone was roughly 20% narrower at its midpoint than at its widest point.
The lower end of the upper arm bone was larger than the upper end and featured three joint surfaces, one of which formed a 120° angle with the surface for the forearm bone.
The upper part of the hip bone was 1.5 times wider than the lower part near the hip socket, a distinctive feature for this genus.
The fused pelvic bones were uniquely shorter than the thigh bone among members of the Ophthalmosauridae family.
The thigh bone had ends of approximately equal width with a slightly narrower middle shaft.
Arthropterygius possessed a pineal foramen that was proportionately larger than in any other known member of the Ophthalmosauridae family.
Fossils of this genus represent the most complete ichthyosaur remains discovered in the Canadian Arctic.
The genus Arthropterygius was formally described by Maxwell in 2010.
A skull and forefin of an ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaur were described in 2012 from the Neuquén Basin in Argentina.
In 2019, Zverkov and Prilepskaya revised the genus, determining that Janusaurus and Palvennia are junior synonyms of Arthropterygius.
Zverkov and Prilepskaya also recognized the taxon Ichthyosaurus volgensis from Russia as a new species of Arthropterygius, named A. volgensis.
Fossils of A. chrisorum, A. lundi, and A. hoybergeti come from the Slottsmøya Member of the Agardhfjellet Formation.
The seafloor at the Slottsmøya Member site was located about 150 meters below the surface and was relatively oxygen-poor.
Researchers suggest sea ice was likely present at the Slottsmøya site during winter due to its high latitude and the cool Tithonian climate.
The Slottsmøya Member contains fossils of other marine reptiles including Undorosaurus gorodischensis, Nannopterygius borealis, and Brachypterygius sp.
The Slottsmøya Member includes 21 plesiosaurian specimens, with Pliosaurus funkei likely serving as the apex predator.
Four species of Arthropterygius (A. chrisorum, A. volgensis, A. lundi, and A. hoybergeti) are found in the Volga region of Russia.
The species A. thalassonotus is found in the Vaca Muerta Formation of the Neuquén Basin in Patagonia, Argentina.
Maxwell (2010) classified Arthropterygius as the sister taxon to the Argentine ophthalmosaurid Caypullisaurus.
Many recent cladistic analyses classify Arthropterygius as the basalmost member of the family Ophthalmosauridae.

Arthropterygius fossils date from the Kimmeridgian to possibly the Berriasian, though some sources limit the range to the Oxfordian to Tithonian stages (161.5–143.1 Ma), while others note presence in the Volgian stage corresponding to the Tithonian-early Berriasian.
Arthropterygius was found in Canada, Norway, Russia, and Argentina.
Arthropterygius lived during the late Jurassic and possibly into the earliest Cretaceous.
The geological outcrops in Svalbard containing Arthropterygius fossils date to the Volgian stage, roughly corresponding to the Tithonian-early Berriasian.
Fossils of Arthropterygius are found in high-latitude locations across the Northern Hemisphere and one isolated site in Argentina.
Arthropterygius lived from the Oxfordian to the Tithonian stages, between 161.5 and 143.1 million years ago.
It is debated whether the large pineal foramen in Arthropterygius was an adaptation to high-latitude environments.
It is debated whether Janusaurus, Keilhauia, and Palvennia should be treated as synonyms of Arthropterygius, as some studies suggest the evidence does not support this synonymy.
